subject: matric-physical-sciences
description: Matric Physical Sciences skill tree (Grade 12 NSC, CAPS). 16 levels (one per CAPS topic) split across Physics (P1) and Chemistry (P2). 42 atomic skills (condensed from 55 in v1.0 by merging tightly-coupled sub-skills). Items live in data/matric-physical-sciences-question-banks/<skill-id>.json.

levels.title: Newton's Laws and Application of Newton's Laws
levels.description: Three Laws of Motion, free-body diagrams, single-body and connected-body problems, inclined planes, friction.

atomic_skills.title: State Newton's laws and draw free-body diagrams
atomic_skills.description: Recall Newton's First, Second and Third Laws in CAPS-correct wording; identify which law applies to a scenario. Draw a free-body diagram for a single object showing all forces (weight, normal, applied, friction, tension, electric) as labelled vectors from a single point.

error_signatures.description: Confuses Newton's Third Law forces with balanced forces on the same body
error_signatures.example: Says the table's normal force on a book and the book's weight are a Newton's Third Law pair

error_signatures.description: Omits 'unless acted on by a net force' from First Law statement
error_signatures.example: States First Law as 'an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity'

error_signatures.description: Includes forces the body exerts on something else in its FBD
error_signatures.example: Adds 'force of block on table' on the block's FBD

error_signatures.description: Forgets the weight when surface is non-horizontal
error_signatures.example: On inclined plane, omits the mg vector

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Anchor each law to a one-line picture: 1st = no net force ⇒ constant velocity; 2nd = Fnet = ma; 3rd = action-reaction pairs act on DIFFERENT objects. For FBDs: list forces touching or pulling the body, each force is FROM something else ON this body, draw all from a single dot.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Newton's Second Law to a single body on horizontal or vertical surfaces
atomic_skills.description: Calculate acceleration, applied force, friction or normal force using Fnet = ma for one object on a horizontal or vertical surface.

error_signatures.description: Uses weight instead of net force
error_signatures.example: Sets mg = ma, gets a = g for a block being pushed across a floor

error_signatures.description: Treats friction as acting in the direction of motion
error_signatures.example: Adds friction to applied force instead of subtracting

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Sum forces along the direction of motion with consistent signs. Friction always opposes relative motion (or attempted motion). Plug into Fnet = ma.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Newton's Second Law to connected bodies and inclined planes
atomic_skills.description: Solve Fnet = ma problems for: two or more objects linked by an inextensible string/pulley (shared acceleration and tension); a body on an inclined plane with friction (resolve weight into mg sinθ and mg cosθ components).

error_signatures.description: Treats tension as different on the two ends of a single inextensible string
error_signatures.example: Calls the tension on the 2 kg block T₁ and on the 8 kg block T₂

error_signatures.description: Tries to solve one body in isolation without first finding the system acceleration
error_signatures.example: Writes Fnet = m₁a for the 2 kg block using only its own forces

error_signatures.description: Uses mg as the parallel component on an incline instead of mg sinθ
error_signatures.example: Sets the down-slope force to mg directly

error_signatures.description: Swaps sin and cos for the incline components
error_signatures.example: Writes parallel = mg cosθ and perpendicular = mg sinθ

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Connected bodies: treat the system as one mass to get acceleration, then isolate one body to get tension. Same string ⇒ same tension throughout. Inclines: tilt your axes with the slope (x = parallel, y = perpendicular). Weight along slope = mg sinθ, perpendicular = mg cosθ.

levels.title: Vertical Projectile Motion
levels.description: Motion of objects projected vertically under gravity only. Kinematics, v-t and position-t graphs, multi-stage motion (including bounces).

atomic_skills.title: Solve vertical projectile problems with kinematic equations and graphs
atomic_skills.description: Use the equations of motion (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as) with a = -g to find time, displacement, velocity for vertical projectile problems. Read and interpret v-t and position-t graphs to extract displacement, velocity, time of flight, and direction of motion.

error_signatures.description: Uses g = +9.8 with upward-positive sign convention
error_signatures.example: Substitutes a = +9.8 m/s² when upward is positive

error_signatures.description: Picks the wrong kinematic equation for the unknown
error_signatures.example: Uses s = ut + ½at² when only u, v and s are known

error_signatures.description: Reads area under v-t as velocity instead of displacement
error_signatures.example: Calculates the area under v-t to find the final velocity

error_signatures.description: Ignores sign convention when reading velocity below the time axis
error_signatures.example: Reports a -5 m/s reading as 5 m/s upward

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Pick a positive direction (usually upward) and stick to it: a = -9.8 m/s². List u, v, s, a, t; pick the equation that uses three knowns and your one unknown. On graphs: area under v-t = displacement; gradient of v-t = acceleration; negative v = downward motion.

atomic_skills.title: Solve multi-stage vertical motion problems (e.g. bouncing ball)
atomic_skills.description: Track velocity, displacement and time across multiple stages of motion such as a ball thrown up, falling, bouncing, and rising again.

error_signatures.description: Treats the whole trajectory as one stage
error_signatures.example: Applies a single kinematic equation across the bounce instant

error_signatures.description: Flips reference direction mid-problem
error_signatures.example: Switches positive direction after the bounce

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Break motion into stages with a clear start and end for each. Velocity reverses at the bounce; check that final velocity of one stage = initial of the next.

levels.title: Work, Energy and Power
levels.description: Work done by a force, work-energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, power calculations.

atomic_skills.title: Define work, energy and power; calculate power
atomic_skills.description: State CAPS-correct definitions for work, conservative force, non-conservative force, mechanical energy, and power. Compute P = W/t or P = Fv for cars, lifts, pumps, motors (average vs instantaneous power).

error_signatures.description: Defines work as force × distance instead of including the cosine of the angle
error_signatures.example: Says W = Fd, omits the cosθ

error_signatures.description: Confuses conservative and non-conservative forces
error_signatures.example: Lists friction as a conservative force

error_signatures.description: Forgets to convert kW to W before using SI formulas
error_signatures.example: Mixes kW with seconds and joules

error_signatures.description: Uses P = Fv when v is changing
error_signatures.example: Treats average power = F × average v for non-uniform motion

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Work = F·d·cosθ where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Conservative ⇒ path-independent (gravity, spring); non-conservative ⇒ path-dependent (friction). Average power = total work ÷ total time. Instantaneous P = Fv at constant velocity. Always SI units (W, J, s).

atomic_skills.title: Apply the work-energy theorem
atomic_skills.description: Use Wnet = ΔKE to find work done, kinetic energy change, final speed, or net force across a displacement.

error_signatures.description: Sums all individual work contributions wrong (sign convention)
error_signatures.example: Adds friction's work as positive

error_signatures.description: Uses ½mv instead of ½mv² for kinetic energy
error_signatures.example: Writes KE = ½mv

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Net work = sum of (each force's work, with sign). Work by friction is always negative on the moving body. Set Wnet = ½m(v² − u²).

atomic_skills.title: Apply conservation of mechanical energy
atomic_skills.description: Use Ei = Ef (KE + PE conserved) for systems acted on by conservative forces only; identify when the principle does not apply.

error_signatures.description: Applies conservation when friction is present
error_signatures.example: Sets ½mu² + mgh = ½mv² with a frictional surface in the system

error_signatures.description: Uses inconsistent reference for PE
error_signatures.example: Picks two different heights as zero for the same problem

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Check first: are there only conservative forces (gravity, spring)? If friction or applied force does work, use work-energy theorem instead. Pick one reference height and use it everywhere.

levels.title: Momentum and Impulse
levels.description: Linear momentum, conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions, impulse and force-time graphs.

atomic_skills.title: Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and explosions
atomic_skills.description: Define p = mv, state the principle of conservation of linear momentum for an isolated system. Apply Σp_before = Σp_after to elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic collisions and to explosions (one body splits into pieces).

error_signatures.description: Omits the direction sign when adding momenta
error_signatures.example: Adds two opposite-direction momenta as if both were positive

error_signatures.description: Applies conservation when an external net force acts
error_signatures.example: Conserves momentum across a collision where the surface has friction during the collision time

error_signatures.description: Sets KE before = KE after for inelastic collisions
error_signatures.example: Uses energy conservation for two stuck-together bodies

error_signatures.description: Doesn't account for direction reversal post-collision
error_signatures.example: Treats both final velocities as forward when one rebounds

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Momentum is a vector — pick a positive direction. Conservation needs an ISOLATED system: no external net force during the interaction. Write Σp_before = Σp_after with signed velocities. Inelastic ⇒ KE NOT conserved. Perfectly inelastic ⇒ shared final velocity. Sketch directions before and after.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate impulse and apply the impulse-momentum theorem
atomic_skills.description: Use Δp = FΔt (impulse-momentum theorem); read impulse off a force-time graph as the area under the curve.

error_signatures.description: Computes Δp as m(v + u) instead of m(v − u)
error_signatures.example: Treats incoming velocity sign as positive when it should be negative

error_signatures.description: Reads area under F-t as force × time instead of impulse
error_signatures.example: Treats the area as the average force

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Impulse = change in momentum = FΔt = area under F-t. Reversal of velocity makes Δp larger, not smaller. Always use signed velocities relative to chosen positive direction.

levels.title: Doppler Effect
levels.description: Doppler effect for sound (moving source/observer) and light (red shift / blue shift in astronomy).

atomic_skills.title: Explain and apply the Doppler equation for sound
atomic_skills.description: State the Doppler effect and explain qualitatively why frequency shifts up when approaching and down when receding. Use f_L = f_s(v ± v_L)/(v ∓ v_s) to find observed frequency, source frequency, or speed of source/observer.

error_signatures.description: Defines Doppler as 'change in wavelength' without mentioning observer perception
error_signatures.example: Says it's just compression and rarefaction of waves

error_signatures.description: Says the actual source frequency changes
error_signatures.example: Claims the siren itself sounds higher when approaching

error_signatures.description: Wrong sign convention for approach/recede in the equation
error_signatures.example: Subtracts when source is approaching, gets f_L < f_s

error_signatures.description: Swaps numerator and denominator
error_signatures.example: Uses (v ∓ v_s)/(v ± v_L) instead of (v ± v_L)/(v ∓ v_s)

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Doppler effect = apparent change in observed frequency (or wavelength) due to relative motion. Source frequency itself unchanged. Sign rule: approach ⇒ frequency increases. Pick signs so that, when source approaches (v_s in denominator with minus), the denominator shrinks and f_L grows. Verify physically.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the Doppler effect to astronomy (red shift and blue shift)
atomic_skills.description: Interpret red shift (recession, longer wavelength) and blue shift (approach, shorter wavelength) for light from stars and galaxies; relate to expansion of the universe.

error_signatures.description: Reverses red and blue shifts
error_signatures.example: Says a star approaching Earth has a red shift

error_signatures.description: Forgets that distant galaxies are mostly red-shifted (expansion)
error_signatures.example: Predicts blue shift for distant galaxies

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Red shift = light stretched to LONGER wavelength = source moving AWAY. Blue shift = SHORTER wavelength = source moving TOWARDS. Most distant galaxies are red-shifted ⇒ universe expanding.

levels.title: Electrostatics
levels.description: Coulomb's Law, electric fields, combination of electric force with mechanics (FBDs with electrostatic forces).

atomic_skills.title: Apply Coulomb's Law to calculate force between point charges
atomic_skills.description: Use F = kQ₁Q₂/r² to compute the magnitude of the electrostatic force between two point charges; identify whether the force is attractive or repulsive.

error_signatures.description: Forgets to square r in Coulomb's Law
error_signatures.example: Writes F = kQ₁Q₂/r

error_signatures.description: Uses signs of charges to get a 'negative force' and mistakes that for a vector
error_signatures.example: Reports F = -45 N and treats it as direction

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Coulomb's Law gives a magnitude; sign of charges tells you only attractive (opposite) or repulsive (same). Use absolute values and decide direction from geometry. Don't forget r² in the denominator.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate electric field at a point (single and net)
atomic_skills.description: Use E = kQ/r² for a single point charge; combine vector contributions from multiple charges to find the net electric field.

error_signatures.description: Adds field magnitudes when fields point in opposite directions
error_signatures.example: Reports net E as 5+3 = 8 N/C when they oppose

error_signatures.description: Forgets to consider field direction (away from + / toward −)
error_signatures.example: Treats E as a scalar everywhere

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Electric field is a vector. From a + charge, E points OUTWARD; from a − charge, E points INWARD. Add as vectors (components or parallelogram). Same direction ⇒ add magnitudes; opposite ⇒ subtract.

atomic_skills.title: Combine electric force with mechanics (FBDs including electric forces)
atomic_skills.description: Solve problems where a charged object is in equilibrium or accelerating under combined electric, gravitational, normal, tension and friction forces.

error_signatures.description: Treats the electric force as parallel to the surface by default
error_signatures.example: Adds Coulomb force into Fnet along incline without resolving its direction

error_signatures.description: Omits weight when an electric force is present
error_signatures.example: Balances only tension and electric force on a hanging charged sphere

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Treat electric force as another vector on the FBD. Resolve all forces (including weight) along the chosen axes, then apply Newton's Second Law.

levels.title: Electric Circuits
levels.description: EMF, current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's Law, series and parallel circuits, internal resistance, AC quantities (RMS).

atomic_skills.title: Apply Ohm's Law and calculate resistance in series and parallel circuits
atomic_skills.description: State CAPS-correct definitions for EMF, current, potential difference, resistance; apply V = IR. Use R_series = R₁ + R₂ + … and 1/R_parallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; reduce mixed networks step by step.

error_signatures.description: Defines EMF as the voltage measured across the battery terminals
error_signatures.example: Says EMF = terminal voltage even with internal resistance

error_signatures.description: Mixes up V, I, R in V = IR substitution
error_signatures.example: Rearranges to I = V × R

error_signatures.description: Adds parallel resistances directly
error_signatures.example: Computes 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 then reports R = 0.5 Ω instead of inverting

error_signatures.description: Reduces the wrong branch first in a mixed circuit
error_signatures.example: Combines series sections that aren't actually in series

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: EMF = energy supplied per unit charge by the source. Series: same current, voltages add ⇒ R adds. Parallel: same voltage, currents add ⇒ 1/R adds. INVERT 1/R_parallel to get R. Reduce mixed circuits one block at a time.

atomic_skills.title: Solve circuit problems with internal resistance
atomic_skills.description: Use EMF = I(R + r) to find EMF, current, internal resistance, or terminal voltage in circuits with non-ideal cells.

error_signatures.description: Treats EMF and terminal voltage as the same thing
error_signatures.example: Reads voltmeter reading across terminals as EMF when current is flowing

error_signatures.description: Misses that open-circuit voltmeter reading = EMF
error_signatures.example: Calculates EMF from terminal voltage when switch is open

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: EMF = I(R_ext + r). Open switch ⇒ I = 0 ⇒ voltmeter reads EMF. Closed switch ⇒ terminal voltage = EMF − Ir.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate AC quantities (RMS voltage/current, average power, frequency)
atomic_skills.description: Use V_rms = V_max/√2, I_rms = I_max/√2, P_avg = V_rms × I_rms, T = 1/f for AC circuits.

error_signatures.description: Uses V_max in average power instead of V_rms
error_signatures.example: Calculates P_avg = V_max × I_max / 2 incorrectly

error_signatures.description: Confuses peak and RMS values
error_signatures.example: Reports 311 V (peak) as the value a multimeter would read

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: RMS = peak / √2. Multimeters and labels (220 V mains) give RMS. P_avg = V_rms × I_rms = (V_max × I_max)/2 for purely resistive AC.

levels.title: Electromagnetic Induction
levels.description: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws, induced EMF, AC and DC generators and motors.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Faraday's and Lenz's Laws to calculate induced EMF
atomic_skills.description: State Faraday's Law (induced EMF proportional to rate of change of flux) and Lenz's Law (induced current opposes the change). Use EMF = -N × ΔΦ/Δt to find induced EMF when flux, number of turns, or change time varies.

error_signatures.description: Reverses Lenz's Law and says induced current supports the change
error_signatures.example: Says induced current flows in the same direction as the change in flux

error_signatures.description: Forgets the rate-of-change part of Faraday
error_signatures.example: Says EMF is proportional to flux itself

error_signatures.description: Forgets to multiply by N (number of turns)
error_signatures.example: Uses EMF = ΔΦ/Δt for a 50-turn coil

error_signatures.description: Uses Φ instead of ΔΦ
error_signatures.example: Substitutes the final flux value as ΔΦ

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Faraday: EMF = -N × ΔΦ/Δt. The minus sign is Lenz's Law: induced current opposes the change that caused it. Magnet pushed in ⇒ coil acts to push it back out. Always compute ΔΦ = Φ_final − Φ_initial including signs. Multiply by N for multi-turn coils.

atomic_skills.title: Describe AC and DC generators and motors
atomic_skills.description: Identify components (coil, brushes, slip rings vs split-ring commutator), explain how each produces AC or DC output (generator) or converts current to motion (motor).

error_signatures.description: Confuses slip rings with split-ring commutator
error_signatures.example: Says DC generator uses slip rings

error_signatures.description: Reverses generator vs motor
error_signatures.example: Says generator converts electrical to mechanical energy

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Generator: mechanical ⇒ electrical (turn coil ⇒ EMF). Motor: electrical ⇒ mechanical (current ⇒ rotation). Slip rings ⇒ AC; split-ring commutator (flips contact) ⇒ DC.

levels.title: Photons and Spectra
levels.description: Photoelectric effect, work function, threshold frequency, maximum kinetic energy; emission and absorption spectra.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the photoelectric effect (work function, threshold frequency, max KE)
atomic_skills.description: Describe the photoelectric effect. Use E = hf, W₀ = hf₀ and E_k(max) = hf − W₀ to find work function, threshold frequency, or maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons given incident frequency or wavelength.

error_signatures.description: Says intensity (brightness) increases the kinetic energy of emitted electrons
error_signatures.example: Predicts brighter light = faster electrons

error_signatures.description: Uses wavelength instead of frequency in E = hf
error_signatures.example: Substitutes λ for f in E = hf

error_signatures.description: Adds W₀ instead of subtracting in E_k formula
error_signatures.example: Writes E_k = hf + hf₀

error_signatures.description: Reports negative E_k when f < f₀ instead of recognising no emission
error_signatures.example: Reports a -2.1 eV kinetic energy

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Photoelectric: light frequency f must exceed threshold f₀ to release electrons. Above threshold, intensity changes NUMBER of electrons, not their KE. Energy in (hf) minus energy needed to escape (W₀) = leftover KE. If hf < W₀, no electrons emitted at all. Use c = fλ to convert.

atomic_skills.title: Explain emission and absorption spectra
atomic_skills.description: Describe how line emission and absorption spectra arise from electron transitions between discrete energy levels; identify which element from a spectrum.

error_signatures.description: Says emission spectrum is continuous
error_signatures.example: Describes hydrogen emission as a smooth rainbow

error_signatures.description: Confuses emission and absorption directions
error_signatures.example: Says absorption is when electron drops from higher to lower energy level

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Emission: electron drops from high to low energy level ⇒ photon released at that exact ΔE ⇒ bright line. Absorption: photon absorbed pushes electron up ⇒ dark line at that wavelength. Both are LINE spectra, not continuous.

levels.title: Gravitation
levels.description: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation; weight and acceleration due to gravity g.

atomic_skills.title: Apply Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
atomic_skills.description: Use F = GMm/r² to find gravitational force between two masses; analyse how the force changes when masses or separation change.

error_signatures.description: Forgets to square r in the denominator
error_signatures.example: Writes F = GMm/r

error_signatures.description: Doubles r and predicts force halves (instead of quarters)
error_signatures.example: Predicts F → F/2 when r doubles

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: F = GMm/r² — inverse square law. r doubles ⇒ F divides by 4. r halves ⇒ F multiplies by 4. Same applies if one mass changes.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate weight and gravitational acceleration g
atomic_skills.description: Use w = mg and g = GM/r² to find weight on Earth, on another planet, or at altitude; relate to free-fall acceleration.

error_signatures.description: Treats mass as changing with planet
error_signatures.example: Says astronaut's mass is less on the Moon

error_signatures.description: Substitutes r as planet radius from centre incorrectly (uses diameter)
error_signatures.example: Uses diameter as r in g = GM/r²

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Mass stays the same; weight changes with g. g = GM/r² where r is distance from CENTRE of the planet, not surface. Weight = mass × local g.

levels.title: Organic Chemistry
levels.description: IUPAC nomenclature, structural formulae, functional groups, physical properties vs structure/IMF, organic reactions.

atomic_skills.title: Apply IUPAC nomenclature rules to name and identify organic compounds
atomic_skills.description: Name and identify alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, haloalkanes, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters using IUPAC rules (parent chain, substituents, numbering, suffixes).

error_signatures.description: Numbers the chain from the wrong end (gives substituent the higher locant)
error_signatures.example: Names 2-methylpentane as 4-methylpentane

error_signatures.description: Confuses suffix for functional group
error_signatures.example: Names a ketone with -al instead of -one

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Find the longest chain CONTAINING the functional group. Number from the end nearest the principal functional group, then the lowest-locant substituent. Match suffix to functional group: -ane (alkane), -ene (alkene), -yne (alkyne), -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic), -oate (ester).

atomic_skills.title: Draw structural formulae, identify functional groups, homologous series and isomers
atomic_skills.description: Convert between full structural, condensed and molecular formulae. Recognise functional groups for each homologous series and identify a compound's series from its structure. Identify and draw structural isomers (chain, positional, functional).

error_signatures.description: Draws a 'different' isomer that's actually the same molecule rotated
error_signatures.example: Drawing 2-methylpropane and 3-methylpropane as separate isomers

error_signatures.description: Confuses positional isomer with functional isomer
error_signatures.example: Lists propan-1-ol and propanal as positional isomers

error_signatures.description: Mixes up aldehyde (-CHO at end) and ketone (>C=O in middle)
error_signatures.example: Calls a chain-end C=O a ketone

error_signatures.description: Misidentifies an ester by missing the -COO- linkage
error_signatures.example: Reads R-COO-R' as an alcohol next to a carboxylic acid

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Same molecular formula, different connectivity = isomer. Chain (branch position), positional (functional group on different carbon), functional (different functional group entirely, e.g. alcohol vs ether). Memorise functional groups visually: -OH (alcohol), -CHO at end (aldehyde), -C(=O)- middle (ketone), -COOH (carboxylic), -COO- (ester linkage), -X (haloalkane), C=C (alkene), C≡C (alkyne).

atomic_skills.title: Relate physical properties to molecular structure and intermolecular forces
atomic_skills.description: Predict and explain trends in boiling point, melting point, viscosity, vapour pressure based on chain length, branching, and functional groups (IMF strength).

error_signatures.description: Says longer chain has WEAKER IMF because lighter per atom
error_signatures.example: Predicts pentane has lower boiling point than butane

error_signatures.description: Ignores branching effect on boiling point
error_signatures.example: Treats 2,2-dimethylpropane and n-pentane as identical

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Longer chain ⇒ more surface area ⇒ stronger London forces ⇒ higher boiling point. Branching ⇒ less contact ⇒ weaker London ⇒ lower bp. Hydrogen bonding (-OH, -NH) >> dipole-dipole > London.

atomic_skills.title: Predict products of organic reactions (substitution, addition, elimination, esterification, oxidation)
atomic_skills.description: Identify reaction type and predict products for haloalkane substitution/elimination, alkene addition, alcohol elimination/oxidation, carboxylic-acid + alcohol esterification.

error_signatures.description: Reverses addition and elimination
error_signatures.example: Calls C=C + H₂ → CH-CH an elimination

error_signatures.description: Forgets to remove H₂O in esterification
error_signatures.example: Writes ester product without showing water loss

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Substitution: swap one group for another (no double bonds change). Addition: C=C or C≡C becomes saturated. Elimination: lose a small molecule (HX or H₂O) and form C=C. Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst).

levels.title: Electrochemistry
levels.description: Galvanic and electrolytic cells, redox half-reactions, standard electrode potentials, cell EMF calculations.

atomic_skills.title: Write balanced redox half-reactions and net cell reactions
atomic_skills.description: Identify oxidation and reduction half-reactions; balance for atoms and charge; combine into the net cell reaction.

error_signatures.description: Doesn't balance charge by adding electrons
error_signatures.example: Writes Fe → Fe²⁺ without the 2e⁻

error_signatures.description: Adds the same number of electrons on both sides of the net equation
error_signatures.example: Combines half-reactions without cancelling matched electrons

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Oxidation = lose electrons (electrons on RIGHT). Reduction = gain electrons (electrons on LEFT). Balance atoms first, then charge with electrons. Multiply each half so electrons cancel when added.

atomic_skills.title: Describe and analyse galvanic and electrolytic cells
atomic_skills.description: For galvanic cells (spontaneous): identify anode (oxidation, NEG terminal), cathode (reduction, POS terminal); write cell notation; describe electron and ion flow. For electrolytic cells (non-spontaneous): identify anode (oxidation, POS terminal — opposite of galvanic), cathode (reduction, NEG terminal); describe electroplating, refining of copper, and electrolysis of NaCl.

error_signatures.description: Swaps anode polarity convention between galvanic and electrolytic
error_signatures.example: Says galvanic anode is positive

error_signatures.description: Says electrons flow through the salt bridge
error_signatures.example: Draws electron flow through the salt bridge instead of external wire

error_signatures.description: Uses galvanic polarity convention for electrolytic cell
error_signatures.example: Calls the electrolytic anode negative

error_signatures.description: Says the electrolytic cell produces its own current
error_signatures.example: Treats an electrolytic cell like a battery

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Both cell types: oxidation at anode, reduction at cathode. Galvanic (spontaneous): anode = NEG, cathode = POS; electrons flow external wire from anode to cathode; ions flow through salt bridge. Electrolytic (non-spontaneous, needs external EMF): anode = POS, cathode = NEG; external battery DRIVES the reaction.

atomic_skills.title: Use standard electrode potentials to predict and calculate cell EMF
atomic_skills.description: Look up E° values from the table; predict which species is oxidised/reduced; calculate E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (using the reduction-potential convention).

error_signatures.description: Subtracts the reverse way (anode − cathode)
error_signatures.example: Reports a negative E°cell for a spontaneous cell

error_signatures.description: Reverses sign of E° when half-reaction is written as oxidation
error_signatures.example: Changes E° sign in the cell EMF calc

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: All E° values in the table are reduction potentials. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (both as reduction values). Positive E°cell ⇒ spontaneous (galvanic). Negative E°cell ⇒ non-spontaneous (electrolytic).

levels.title: Chemical Equilibrium
levels.description: Dynamic equilibrium, equilibrium constant Kc, Le Chatelier's Principle, ICE-table calculations, industrial applications (Haber, Contact).

atomic_skills.title: Define dynamic equilibrium and write Kc expressions
atomic_skills.description: State the meaning of dynamic chemical equilibrium; write Kc expressions for given reversible reactions (excluding pure solids/liquids).

error_signatures.description: Includes solids or pure liquids in Kc expression
error_signatures.example: Includes [CaCO₃] in Kc for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

error_signatures.description: Says rates are zero at equilibrium
error_signatures.example: Defines equilibrium as 'no reaction happening'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Dynamic equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate (both > 0). Kc = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff for gases and aqueous species only. Pure solids and pure liquids excluded (activity = 1).

atomic_skills.title: Apply Le Chatelier's Principle and explain industrial processes
atomic_skills.description: Predict direction of equilibrium shift when concentration, pressure, volume, or temperature changes; account for catalyst (no shift, faster equilibration). Explain how temperature, pressure, and catalyst choices in the Haber, Contact, and Ostwald processes are dictated by equilibrium and rate considerations.

error_signatures.description: Says a catalyst shifts equilibrium
error_signatures.example: Predicts more product when catalyst is added

error_signatures.description: Reverses pressure shift
error_signatures.example: Predicts shift to MORE moles of gas when pressure increases

error_signatures.description: Says high temperature increases yield for exothermic forward reactions
error_signatures.example: Claims Haber should run at very high T for more NH₃

error_signatures.description: Confuses Haber, Contact, Ostwald products
error_signatures.example: Says the Contact process makes ammonia

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Add concentration ⇒ shift away from added species. Increase pressure ⇒ shift to FEWER moles of gas. Increase temperature ⇒ shift in the ENDOTHERMIC direction. Catalyst: no shift, just faster. Haber (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, exothermic): high P (good); moderate T (compromise); Fe catalyst. Contact: SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄. Ostwald: NH₃ → NO → HNO₃.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate Kc using ICE (Initial-Change-Equilibrium) tables
atomic_skills.description: Build ICE tables from initial concentrations and reaction stoichiometry; solve for Kc or for equilibrium concentrations given Kc.

error_signatures.description: Forgets to apply stoichiometric ratios in the 'Change' row
error_signatures.example: Subtracts x from each reactant regardless of coefficient

error_signatures.description: Uses moles instead of concentrations in Kc
error_signatures.example: Substitutes mol values directly without dividing by V

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: ICE rows: Initial (start concentrations), Change (±stoich × x), Equilibrium (I + C). Kc uses concentrations [mol/dm³], not moles. Always check x makes physical sense (positive, < initial).

levels.title: Acids and Bases
levels.description: Brønsted-Lowry definitions, conjugate pairs, pH/pOH/Kw calculations, strong vs weak acids/bases, titrations.

atomic_skills.title: Apply the Brønsted-Lowry definition and identify conjugate acid-base pairs
atomic_skills.description: Identify acid, base, conjugate acid, conjugate base in a Brønsted-Lowry reaction; identify amphiprotic substances.

error_signatures.description: Identifies a substance as both acid and base in the same direction of reaction
error_signatures.example: Says NH₃ is acid AND base on the same side

error_signatures.description: Forgets the H⁺ transfer in identifying the conjugate
error_signatures.example: Calls HCl and Cl₂ a conjugate pair instead of HCl/Cl⁻

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Brønsted-Lowry acid = H⁺ DONOR. Base = H⁺ ACCEPTOR. Conjugate pair = differs by one H⁺. Amphiprotic = can donate OR accept (e.g. HCO₃⁻, H₂O).

atomic_skills.title: Calculate pH, pOH, [H⁺], [OH⁻] using Kw
atomic_skills.description: Convert between [H⁺], [OH⁻], pH and pOH using pH = -log[H⁺], pH + pOH = 14, [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1×10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C.

error_signatures.description: Drops the negative sign in pH definition
error_signatures.example: Writes pH = log[H⁺]

error_signatures.description: Forgets to take antilog when going from pH back to [H⁺]
error_signatures.example: Reports [H⁺] = 3 for pH = 3

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: pH = -log[H⁺]. [H⁺] = 10^(-pH). pH + pOH = 14 (at 25°C). Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1×10⁻¹⁴. Use the chain: if you have one, you can get all four.

atomic_skills.title: Distinguish strong vs weak acids/bases and apply Ka/Kb
atomic_skills.description: Classify acids/bases as strong (fully dissociated) or weak; relate degree of ionisation to Ka/Kb; use conductivity, pH, and concentration comparisons.

error_signatures.description: Equates strong with concentrated (or weak with dilute)
error_signatures.example: Calls a 0.01 mol/dm³ HCl 'weak'

error_signatures.description: Lists CH₃COOH as a strong acid
error_signatures.example: Treats acetic acid as fully ionised

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Strong/weak = degree of IONISATION. Concentrated/dilute = AMOUNT in a given volume. Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first). Strong bases: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂. Most others are weak.

atomic_skills.title: Solve titration calculations and select indicators
atomic_skills.description: Use n(acid) × stoichiometric ratio = n(base) (or pH at equivalence) to find unknown concentration, volume, or molar mass; select indicator based on type of acid/base.

error_signatures.description: Ignores stoichiometric ratio when not 1:1
error_signatures.example: Treats H₂SO₄ + NaOH as 1:1

error_signatures.description: Picks indicator with pH range mismatched to the equivalence pH
error_signatures.example: Uses methyl orange for a weak acid + strong base titration

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: c_a × V_a × n_a = c_b × V_b × n_b (n = mole coefficient). Equivalence pH: strong-strong ≈ 7; weak acid + strong base > 7 (phenolphthalein); strong acid + weak base < 7 (methyl orange).

levels.title: Reaction Rate
levels.description: Definition of reaction rate, collision theory, factors affecting rate, rate calculations from data and graphs.

atomic_skills.title: Define reaction rate, apply collision theory, and explain factors affecting rate
atomic_skills.description: State reaction rate as change in amount per unit time. Explain qualitatively using collision theory (frequency, energy, orientation). Predict and explain the effect of concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst (and pressure for gases) on the rate of a reaction.

error_signatures.description: Omits 'effective' or activation-energy requirement from collision theory
error_signatures.example: Says any collision produces a reaction

error_signatures.description: Confuses 'effective collision' with 'any collision with enough energy'
error_signatures.example: Ignores orientation factor

error_signatures.description: Says a catalyst increases the energy of reactant particles
error_signatures.example: Claims catalyst raises particle KE

error_signatures.description: Says higher temperature lowers activation energy
error_signatures.example: Confuses 'more particles exceed Ea' with 'Ea is lower'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Rate = change in concentration per unit time. Effective collision needs sufficient KE (≥ Ea) AND correct orientation. Catalyst LOWERS Ea by providing an alternative pathway (doesn't change KE of particles). Higher T ⇒ more particles have KE ≥ Ea ⇒ faster rate. Higher concentration / smaller particles / higher pressure ⇒ more frequent collisions.

atomic_skills.title: Calculate reaction rates from data and graphs
atomic_skills.description: Find average and instantaneous rates from concentration-time, mass-time, or volume-time graphs; relate rate ratios to stoichiometry.

error_signatures.description: Reports rate as a negative value (for reactants)
error_signatures.example: Says rate = -0.05 mol/s as the final answer

error_signatures.description: Forgets stoichiometric coefficients when relating rates of different species
error_signatures.example: Says rate of N₂ consumption = rate of NH₃ production

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Rate is always reported as a positive value. For aA + bB → cC + dD: -(1/a)d[A]/dt = -(1/b)d[B]/dt = +(1/c)d[C]/dt = +(1/d)d[D]/dt. Average rate = slope of secant; instantaneous = slope of tangent.

levels.title: Intermolecular Forces
levels.description: Identifying types of intermolecular forces; relating IMF to physical properties (boiling/melting points, vapour pressure, surface tension, solubility).

atomic_skills.title: Identify intermolecular forces in compounds
atomic_skills.description: Identify London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding interactions in a given compound from its structure.

error_signatures.description: Says all polar molecules have hydrogen bonding
error_signatures.example: Lists HCl as having hydrogen bonds

error_signatures.description: Lists London forces only for non-polar molecules
error_signatures.example: Says polar molecules have no London forces

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: London (dispersion): in ALL molecules. Dipole-dipole: in polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding: when H is bonded to N, O or F. A polar molecule has both London + dipole-dipole; an H-bonder has all three.

atomic_skills.title: Relate intermolecular forces to physical properties
atomic_skills.description: Predict and explain trends in boiling point, melting point, vapour pressure, surface tension, and solubility based on IMF strength.

error_signatures.description: Says stronger IMF = HIGHER vapour pressure
error_signatures.example: Predicts water has higher vapour pressure than ethanol

error_signatures.description: Forgets molecular size when comparing two compounds with same IMF type
error_signatures.example: Predicts methane and propane have the same boiling point

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Stronger IMF ⇒ harder to break apart ⇒ higher boiling/melting point, LOWER vapour pressure, higher surface tension. Within same IMF type, bigger molecule ⇒ stronger London ⇒ higher bp.
